note: Butcher's 'represented' (a horse) was changed to 'shown'; the style note keeps 'represent'.
replacement: The poet is an imitator, like a painter or any other artist, so he must always imitate one of three kinds of objects — things as they were or are, things as people say or think they are, or things as they ought to be. He expresses them in language, using either current terms or, it may be, rare words or metaphors. There are also many modifications of language, and we allow these to poets. Add to this that the standard of correctness is not the same in poetry as in politics, any more than it is the same in poetry as in any other art. Within the art of poetry itself there are two kinds of faults: those that touch its essence, and those that are accidental. Suppose a poet has chosen to imitate something, <but has imitated it incorrectly> through lack of capacity. Then the error is inherent in the poetry. But suppose the failure comes from a wrong choice — he has represented a horse as throwing out both its off legs at once, or has made technical inaccuracies in medicine, for example, or in some other art. Then the error is not essential to the poetry. These are the points of view from which we should consider and answer the objections the critics raise.

replacement: It is superior, and the reasons are these. It has all the epic elements — it may even use the epic meter. It also has music and spectacular effects as important accessories, and these produce the most vivid of pleasures. Further, it is vivid in reading as well as in representation. Moreover, it attains the end of the art within narrower limits, and a concentrated effect is more pleasurable than one that is spread over a long time and so diluted. Consider, for example, what would become of the Oedipus of Sophocles if it were cast in a form as long as the Iliad. Once more, the Epic imitation has less unity, and this is shown by the fact that any Epic poem supplies subjects for several tragedies. So when the poet adopts a story of strict unity, he must either tell it briefly and make it seem truncated, or, if he follows the Epic canon of length, make it seem weak and watery. <Such length implies some loss of unity,> by which I mean that the poem is built out of several actions, as the Iliad and the Odyssey are, with many such parts, each having a certain magnitude of its own. Yet these poems are as perfectly constructed as possible, and each is, as far as can be attained, an imitation of a single action.
